description: Soy Irene Salomé Romero Tucto, Asesora del equipo GOOD AYNI NOVA de Cajamarca-Perú, estudiantes apasionados por la ciencia, tecnología, innovación y exploración espacial. En NASA Space Apps 2026 conectaremos los desafíos de las comunidades andinas con futuras misiones a la Luna o Marte, usando datos abiertos de la NASA. Valoramos la creatividad, interés en programación, inteligencia artificial, diseño, análisis de datos, comunicación científica, trabajo colaborativo, investigación y aprendizaje.

1. Summary
GOOD AYNI NOVA is a student-led geospatial initiative from Dos de Mayo School in Cajamarca, Perú. Our team built AYNI-ANALOG SatLab, an interactive web prototype that pairs terrestrial and planetary maps to explore potential Earth analog sites for Moon and Mars surface experiments. Rather than just looking for landscapes that visually resemble other worlds, the tool helps students identify which measurable terrain properties actually matter for a given test.
Through a side-by-side interface, users can explore maps, customize evaluation criteria, inspect transparent site rankings, record field observations, and export their findings in CSV format. For Earth visualization, the prototype integrates NASA GIBS ASTER GDEM shaded-relief imagery alongside live elevation queries powered by the Open-Meteo API (using Copernicus DEM GLO-90 data), while planetary metrics currently rely on baseline demonstrative values.
Building on this working web prototype, we are developing the AYNI-ANALOG App as a future multilingual, cross-platform tool. Our goal is to support hands-on science education, encourage transparent preliminary terrain analysis, and—once fully validated—assist early-stage research planning. Throughout the project, we clearly separate working features from future goals, offering an exploratory learning platform rather than a certified tool for operational space missions.
details:
1. Summary

GOOD AYNI NOVA is a student-led geospatial initiative from Dos de Mayo School in Cajamarca, Perú. Our team built AYNI-ANALOG SatLab, an interactive web prototype that pairs terrestrial and planetary maps to explore potential Earth analog sites for Moon and Mars surface experiments. Rather than just looking for landscapes that visually resemble other worlds, the tool helps students identify which measurable terrain properties actually matter for a given test.

Through a side-by-side interface, users can explore maps, customize evaluation criteria, inspect transparent site rankings, record field observations, and export their findings in CSV format. For Earth visualization, the prototype integrates NASA GIBS ASTER GDEM shaded-relief imagery alongside live elevation queries powered by the Open-Meteo API (using Copernicus DEM GLO-90 data), while planetary metrics currently rely on baseline demonstrative values.

Building on this working web prototype, we are developing the AYNI-ANALOG App as a future multilingual, cross-platform tool. Our goal is to support hands-on science education, encourage transparent preliminary terrain analysis, and—once fully validated—assist early-stage research planning. Throughout the project, we clearly separate working features from future goals, offering an exploratory learning platform rather than a certified tool for operational space missions.

The project started with a simple question from the Peruvian Andes: ¿could our local landscapes help students understand the challenges exploration robots face on the Moon or Mars? We wanted to make planetary mapping accessible without needing expensive or specialized gear. By building a web-based tool, students can explore a site, ask their own scientific questions, adjust their analysis, and save their findings. This approach is inspired by ayni, an Andean concept of cooperation and reciprocity, which guides how we share knowledge—though it does not represent a new scientific law or an official partnership with NASA.

2. Problem statement and justification

Testing space technology on Earth requires choosing sites that match specific experimental needs. Two landscapes might look alike on the surface, yet differ greatly in slope, roughness, accessibility, or material properties, not to mention environmental factors like gravity, atmosphere, temperature, and radiation. On top of that, public geographic data is often hard for beginners to read and interpret. An easy-to-use educational screening tool can bridge this gap by helping users compare key terrain features, spot limitations early, and ask better questions before doing fieldwork. While the Andes offer a meaningful local starting point for this work, the project does not assume that every Andean site is a direct planetary analog.

Research question: ¿How can user-friendly geospatial tools help students compare Earth and planetary terrain features to design responsible preliminary field tests?

3. General goal: Develop and validate a transparent geospatial comparison tool, taking it from the working SatLab web prototype to the full AYNI-ANALOG App.

4. Specific objectives:

  • Display both terrestrial and planetary terrain scenarios clearly.
  • Compare key variables such as slope, roughness, elevation, and site accessibility.
  • Allow users to set their own evaluation criteria and understand the resulting rankings.
  • Record underlying assumptions, field observations, and data limitations.
  • Support importing and exporting data records in CSV format.
  • Add recommendations tailored to specific technology tests in upcoming modules.
  • Expand accessibility by building a multilingual mobile application in the future.
  • Validate the datasets and methods through user testing and expert feedback.

5. What the web prototype does: component-by-component walkthrough

  • A. Opening screen: Introduces the GOOD AYNI NOVA team identity, project challenge, and motto, along with a direct button to launch the SatLab workspace.
  • B. Two-world laboratory: Uses a split-screen map view. The left panel displays selected Moon and Mars scenarios, while the right panel centers on Peru with NASA GIBS ASTER shaded relief and an alternative satellite imagery layer.
  • C. Place selection: Includes preset Peruvian sites—Cumbe Mayo, Alto Perú, El Gavilán, La Joya, and Ocucaje—while also letting users click anywhere on the map to query new terrestrial elevation data.
  • D. Terrain indicators: Calculates and displays four core metrics for each location: elevation, slope, surface roughness, and an estimated accessibility score.
  • E. Criteria selection: Lets users toggle any of the four indicators on or off, or apply quick presets depending on their comparison goals.
  • F. Candidate ranking: Filters between natural landscapes and populated areas, sorting the candidate sites dynamically based on the selected indicators and scores.
  • G. Analysis panel: Helps users interpret the data through an overall circular score, individual metric bars, side-by-side comparison charts, and a sample experiment idea.
  • H. Research notes: Provides a built-in notepad where students can write down their observations, assumptions, and field caveats.
  • I. CSV manager: Allows users to export their rankings and notes as a CSV file, or reload previous sessions to continue their work later.
  • J. Methods and sources: Explains how the scoring heuristic works, provides links to scientific and mapping references, and credits the school and faculty advisor. A closing note reminds users that all outputs are exploratory and points them toward the upcoming mobile app.

6. Technology, design, data flow and the algorithm

The web prototype runs directly in the browser using HTML5 for layout, CSS3 for responsive styling, and vanilla JavaScript for state management and calculations, paired with Leaflet 1.9.4 for interactive maps. Its interface organizes data through dark blue panels, highlighted metric readouts, filter checkboxes, ranking cards, comparison charts, pop-up modals, and CSV export tools.

When a user selects new coordinates on Earth, the app queries nine nearby elevation points via the Open-Meteo Elevation API (which draws from the Copernicus DEM GLO-90 dataset) and uses Nominatim to fetch basic geographic context. From those nine elevation samples, the script estimates local slope and surface roughness, combining them with predefined planetary and terrestrial baseline values.

To rank sites, the tool relies on a simple, transparent heuristic rather than a complex black-box model. Under the default setup—combining slope, roughness, and accessibility—the weights are split 40%, 40%, and 20%, respectively; if the user picks any other combination of criteria, the active indicators are averaged equally. These scores are meant to show how weighted criteria work in practice, not to certify real-world site suitability or mission success. In its current browser-based form, the prototype operates entirely on the client side without a Python/Streamlit backend or physical hardware integration.

7. Innovation and why it is distinctive

Space agencies like NASA already rely on terrestrial analog sites, planetary mapping, and rover testbeds for mission planning. What sets this student project apart is how it brings together an Andean geographic focus, a side-by-side two-world map view, customizable and transparent terrain comparisons, guided field-test prompts, and exportable research records in one accessible classroom tool.

Looking ahead, our roadmap focuses on four main upgrades: screening sites for specific types of experiments, displaying uncertainty ranges alongside results, grounding comparisons in documented planetary topographic datasets, and building a shared network for local field observations. For now, these features remain planned concepts rather than validated modules in the current prototype.

8. Benefits and possible users

Right now, the prototype gives students and teachers a hands-on way to practice geospatial reasoning, read topographic maps, evaluate measurement uncertainty, and record structured terrain comparisons. Over time, as the platform matures, it can also support universities, student robotics labs planning small-scale field trials, local science clubs, and research teams looking for a simple preliminary site-screening aid.

With proper validation, these same comparison methods could even help educational programs study rough-terrain robotics or remote land inspection here on Earth. However, because the software is strictly an exploratory learning tool, it should never be used to make certified decisions in safety, mining, rescue operations, civil engineering, or actual space mission planning.

9. Final product: AYNI-ANALOG App (in development)

The current SatLab web prototype is just the first stage of the project. Our final goal is the AYNI-ANALOG App, a cross-platform application currently in development for smartphones, tablets, and desktop computers.

To make the tool truly accessible for classrooms and field teams, we plan to introduce several key upgrades:

  • A clearer, step-by-step onboarding guide for new users.
  • Full multilingual support across the entire interface.
  • Verified terrestrial and planetary datasets paired with visible data-quality indicators.
  • Optional offline mode so students can save and review reports without an internet connection.
  • Built-in educational experiment guides and a collaborative space to share documented field observations.

Because the app is still actively being built, cross-device testing, app-store publication, and a wider public release remain future development milestones rather than completed features.

10. Sustainability

To keep the project sustainable over time without limiting student access, we propose a tiered model that has not yet been tested in the market. Core educational features would remain free for individual learners, while optional institutional licenses could offer schools and universities classroom management tools and teaching resources. Once the platform passes technical validation, we could also introduce specialized modules for research teams.

Before taking any commercial steps, our next phase will focus on customer discovery with local schools, university programs, and student robotics clubs to understand their real needs. At this early stage, the project has no active sales, paid subscriptions, external clients, or proven market traction. Moving toward a public launch will also require carefully reviewing third-party mapping and data licenses, estimating cloud-hosting and maintenance costs, and setting up strong data privacy safeguards and user support.

11. Testing, evidence and validation plan

Currently verifiable interface features

Right now, anyone interacting with the web prototype can directly test and verify its core software functions: switching between lunar and Martian scenarios, exploring the map of Peru, adjusting comparison criteria, watching site rankings update in real time, writing research notes, and exporting or reloading CSV reports. While these steps confirm that the user interface works as intended, they demonstrate software functionality rather than scientific predictive accuracy.

Planned functional software tests

To verify technical stability across different devices and conditions, we have outlined a series of functional checks:

  • Open the web application across at least two different web browsers to confirm consistent behavior.
  • Verify that base maps and shaded-relief tiles load reliably.
  • Switch between planetary bodies and confirm that the active scenario is recorded accurately.
  • Evaluate the same terrestrial location under two different criteria presets and document how the rankings shift.
  • Click new coordinates on Earth to inspect the elevation API response and verify fallback handling if a request fails.
  • Export a CSV report, reload it into the app, and confirm that all criteria settings and notes are restored intact.
  • Check interface accessibility and responsive layout behavior on smaller mobile screens.

Planned scientific validation steps

Moving from an educational prototype to a scientifically vetted tool requires deeper technical verification. Our validation roadmap includes documenting the exact source and spatial resolution of every dataset, integrating an official NASA planetary elevation product, independently recalculating all slope and roughness descriptors, verifying coordinate reference systems, quantifying measurement uncertainty, comparing software outputs against expert field observations, and testing repeatability across sessions. At this stage, we do not claim measured predictive accuracy, guaranteed API uptime, completed user-study metrics, or validated analog-site classifications.

12. Use of AI tools and transparency

Generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, were used during the project workflow to help draft and revise documentation, brainstorm interface and code improvements, and prepare bilingual explanations. Where AI-assisted illustrations or animated concepts are included in our final deliverables, they are clearly labeled to distinguish them from human-made graphics and official satellite imagery. For narrated audio and video assets—such as early tests explored with tools like Runway—we only credit specific generation platforms once their exact production source is verified, and we ensure all synthetic media carries the disclosures or metadata required by event guidelines.

Inside the SatLab web application itself, no machine learning models, neural networks, or automated predictive AI are used. As documented in our source code, terrain comparisons rely strictly on a transparent, rules-based mathematical heuristic rather than trained algorithms or NASA-certified AI systems. Additionally, AI-assisted code segments are noted in our repository documentation, and we strictly avoid placing NASA trademarks or official logos onto any AI-generated visuals.

13. Team responsibilities

  • Scientific coordination and academic supervision: Prof. Irene Salomé Romero Tucto (Faculty Advisor, Physics and Chemistry).
  • Student research lead: (Christopher Bruno Estraver Pérez) — Coordinates the research question, field notes, and scientific citations.
  • Web and software lead: (Diego Gabriel Rojas Aguirre) — Oversees interface development, version control, and cross-browser testing.
  • Data and validation lead: (Mateo Alessandro Saucedo Carrasco) — Manages dataset sources, evaluation criteria, experiment design, and uncertainty documentation.
  • Demo and communication lead: (Yosmel Eduar Chilón Marín) — Leads video production, bilingual captions, public communication, and media permissions.
  • Responsible for the application: (Jose Daylin Aliaga Chuquiruna). He supervises the development of interfaces, version control and testing of the application.

14. Conclusion and scientific commitment

GOOD AYNI NOVA delivers a working educational software prototype along with a clear roadmap toward a broader platform. Rather than claiming that the Andes are a direct replica of the Moon or Mars, the project encourages students to think critically—asking which terrain properties can truly be compared, what kind of field experiments make sense, and what evidence is still needed.

Today, users can already explore the functional SatLab web experience, while the full AYNI-ANALOG App moves forward in active development. By integrating validated NASA planetary datasets, conducting thorough user testing, accounting for measurement uncertainty, and maintaining transparent licensing, this initiative can grow into a reliable open-education research tool—guided by our core motto: Two Worlds, One Mission.

Organizar las actividades de investigación, diseño, programación, implementación, validación y presentación del proyecto GOOD AYNI NOVA, desde el desarrollo de la plataforma web AYNI-ANALOG SatLab hasta su evolución hacia el aplicativo multiplataforma AYNI-ANALOG App, destinado a facilitar el análisis de terrenos terrestres y planetarios para usuarios de diferentes partes del mundo.

5. Resultados esperados

Al finalizar el cronograma, se espera contar con una aplicación multiplataforma capaz de ampliar las funciones de SatLab, incorporar información científica verificable, facilitar comparaciones de terrenos y generar informes accesibles.

La propuesta también contempla pruebas con usuarios, documentación de limitaciones científicas y una evaluación inicial de su posible sostenibilidad comercial.

6. Conclusión

El cronograma de GOOD AYNI NOVA establece una ruta progresiva para transformar una propuesta estudiantil en una herramienta tecnológica con proyección internacional.

La plataforma web constituye el punto de partida; el siguiente desafío es desarrollar, probar y validar AYNI-ANALOG App, con el propósito de acercar la ciencia planetaria a estudiantes, investigadores y comunidades de distintas regiones del mundo.

GOOD AYNI NOVA — De Cajamarca para el mundo. De los Andes a la Luna. Dos mundos, una misión.
